patent_evidence.US8672871B2_claim_1: A method for draining CSF from the subarachnoid space into the venous system, comprising: providing a shunt having a one-way valve located at the first end... draining CSF through the tip and out through the valve into the venous system
key_elements: One-way valve at the venous end
CSF drains from subarachnoid space to venous system
The valve prevents retrograde venous blood flow into the CSF space
patent_evidence.what_the_valve_does: The one-way valve prevents backflow of venous blood into the CSF space. It opens when CSF pressure exceeds venous pressure (positive ICP-venous gradient) and closes when venous pressure exceeds CSF pressure (preventing retrograde flow).
patent_evidence.what_the_valve_does_NOT_do: The patent does NOT describe: (1) adjustable opening pressure, (2) posture-responsive resistance, (3) flow-rate limitation, (4) patient-specific pressure-differential adaptation. The valve is a simple one-way (check) valve.

clinical_evidence.STRIDE_trial: STRIDE pivotal trial enrollment completed. 97% of subjects (29/30) experienced improvement in NPH symptoms. 0 serious adverse events related to the device through 90-day follow-up.
clinical_evidence.follow_up_duration: 90 days (short-term — long-term over-drainage data NOT yet available)
clinical_evidence.population: Elderly NPH patients (specific population — over-drainage risk may differ from pediatric or post-hemorrhagic populations)
clinical_evidence.key_gap: 90-day follow-up is too short to assess over-drainage complications (subdural hematomas and slit ventricle syndrome typically develop over months to years). The eShunt's long-term over-drainage profile is UNKNOWN.

protocol_description.mechanism: The eShunt uses the naturally occurring CSF-to-venous pressure gradient to regulate flow. When ICP > P_venous, the one-way valve opens and CSF drains. When P_venous >= ICP (e.g., during Valsalva), the valve closes.
protocol_description.regulation_type: PASSIVE — the valve responds to the instantaneous pressure differential. It does NOT: sense posture, adjust threshold, limit flow rate, or adapt to patient-specific physiology.
protocol_description.what_it_addresses: Prevents retrograde flow (venous blood entering CSF space). Provides passive drainage when ICP > venous pressure.
protocol_description.what_it_does_NOT_address: Does NOT prevent over-drainage caused by large hydrostatic gradients (upright posture). Does NOT limit flow rate. Does NOT adapt to patient-specific pressure thresholds. Does NOT account for time-varying venous pressure (sleep apnea, Valsalva, posture changes).

residual_failure_matrix.what_it_improves: Allows non-invasive external adjustment of opening pressure. Reduces over-drainage incidence by allowing physician to tune the valve post-implantation.
residual_failure_matrix.what_remains_unresolved: REACTIVE: physician adjusts based on symptoms AFTER over-drainage has already occurred. Cannot prevent the FIRST over-drainage event. Cannot adapt in real-time to posture or venous pressure changes. Patient still over-drains between adjustments.
residual_failure_matrix.evidence_strength: STRONG — widely adopted, multiple RCTs, long track record. Meta-analyses confirm reduced revision rates vs fixed-pressure valves.
residual_failure_matrix.residual_failure: Real-time inability to prevent over-drainage during posture transitions or venous pressure fluctuations

residual_failure_matrix.what_it_improves: Adds posture-dependent resistance. Directly addresses the hydrostatic gradient problem when upright. Reduces over-drainage in standing/sitting patients.
residual_failure_matrix.what_remains_unresolved: Responds to POSTURE, not actual pressure differential. Fixed gravitational threshold set at implantation. Cannot distinguish 'upright and safe' from 'upright and over-draining.' Risk of under-drainage when upright with elevated ICP. Cannot adapt to patient-specific venous pressure physiology.
residual_failure_matrix.evidence_strength: MODERATE-STRONG — clinical studies show reduced over-drainage in upright patients. However, under-drainage complications are reported. Patient selection matters.
residual_failure_matrix.residual_failure: Cannot adapt to patient-specific real-time pressure dynamics. Fixed gravitational threshold may be wrong for individual patients.

residual_failure_matrix.what_it_improves: Limits siphon effect by closing when pressure differential exceeds threshold. 2026 meta-analysis (7 studies, 928 NPH patients) found SIGNIFICANT reduction in subdural hygroma and hematoma.
residual_failure_matrix.what_remains_unresolved: Fixed threshold (not patient-specific). The 2026 meta-analysis found 'overall over-drainage and revision outcomes were NOT significantly different' — meaning the device helps with SOME over-drainage consequences but not all. Does not account for venous pressure dynamics.
residual_failure_matrix.evidence_strength: MODERATE — 2026 meta-analysis is the strongest evidence. Significant for subdural outcomes, but NOT significant for overall over-drainage or revision. This is the CRITICAL finding: the device reduces radiographic over-drainage but not clinical outcomes.
residual_failure_matrix.residual_failure: Over-drainage consequences OTHER than subdural hygroma/hematoma are not reduced. Clinical outcomes (revision, symptoms) not significantly improved.

residual_failure_matrix.what_it_improves: Regulates FLOW rate rather than pressure. Maintains constant drainage rate regardless of pressure differential. Reduces siphon effect.
residual_failure_matrix.what_remains_unresolved: Fixed flow rate — cannot adapt to patient-specific CSF production or changing physiological needs. Risk of under-drainage when CSF production exceeds fixed rate. Risk of over-drainage when production is below fixed rate. Does not account for venous pressure.
residual_failure_matrix.evidence_strength: MODERATE — widely used in Europe. Clinical studies show comparable outcomes to differential-pressure valves with fewer revisions in some populations. However, fixed-flow limitation is well-documented.
residual_failure_matrix.residual_failure: Fixed flow rate is a compromise. Cannot adapt to patient-specific or time-varying drainage needs.

residual_failure_matrix.what_it_improves: Uses the CSF-to-venous pressure gradient for passive drainage. One-way valve prevents retrograde flow. The venous system is a low-pressure, compliant reservoir that naturally limits the pressure differential compared to the peritoneum (VP shunts). This may REDUCE but does NOT ELIMINATE over-drainage risk.
residual_failure_matrix.what_remains_unresolved: The eShunt's one-way valve is a PASSIVE check valve. It does NOT: (1) limit flow rate, (2) adjust opening pressure, (3) respond to posture, (4) adapt to patient-specific physiology, (5) account for time-varying venous pressure (sleep apnea, Valsalva, coughing). When the patient is upright, the hydrostatic gradient between the CSF space (cranial) and the venous sinus (also cranial) is SMALLER than in VP shunts (cranial to peritoneal), but it is NOT ZERO. The eShunt's venous outflow is in the sigmoid sinus — when the patient is upright, venous pressure in the sigmoid sinus can DROP (negative pressure due to gravity-assisted venous drainage), INCREASING the CSF-to-venous gradient and causing over-drainage. The eShunt's 90-day clinical data does NOT cover the time window in which over-drainage complications typically develop (months to years).
residual_failure_matrix.evidence_strength: WEAK for over-drainage — 90-day follow-up is too short. 0 SAEs through 90 days is encouraging but does NOT establish long-term over-drainage safety. The eShunt's passive valve mechanism is fundamentally similar to a differential-pressure valve — it has the SAME theoretical over-drainage risk as any passive pressure-gradient valve.
residual_failure_matrix.residual_failure: The eShunt's passive one-way valve does NOT prevent over-drainage caused by: (a) upright-posture venous pressure drops in the sigmoid sinus, (b) time-varying venous pressure fluctuations (sleep apnea, Valsalva), (c) patient-specific CSF production rates that exceed the passive drainage capacity, (d) the absence of any flow-rate limitation or posture-responsive resistance. The eShunt is a CHECK VALVE, not a FLOW REGULATOR.

residual_failure.failure_statement: All existing CSF shunt technologies — including the eShunt's passive one-way pressure-gradient valve — use FIXED or PASSIVE regulation mechanisms that cannot adapt to patient-specific, time-varying CSF-to-venous pressure dynamics. Specifically: when venous pressure in the drainage target drops (upright posture, sleep apnea, Valsalva release), the pressure differential increases and the shunt drains more CSF than the patient's physiology requires, causing over-drainage. No existing technology — programmable, gravitational, anti-siphon, flow-regulated, or the eShunt's passive check valve — measures and responds to the ACTUAL real-time CSF-to-venous pressure differential in a patient-specific way.
residual_failure.falsifiable_causal_statement: IF a CSF shunt uses a passive or fixed-threshold regulation mechanism (including the eShunt's one-way check valve), AND the patient experiences time-varying venous pressure drops (upright posture, sleep apnea, Valsalva), THEN the shunt will drain more CSF than physiologically required, causing over-drainage complications (subdural hematoma, slit ventricle syndrome) in a clinically significant fraction of patients over a time window of months to years.
residual_failure.what_makes_this_residual:
This failure survives ALL existing technology because:
1. Programmable valves are REACTIVE (adjust after the fact)
2. Gravitational valves respond to POSTURE, not venous pressure
3. Anti-siphon devices use FIXED thresholds (2026 meta-analysis: subdural outcomes improved but overall over-drainage and revision NOT significantly different)
4. Flow-regulated systems use FIXED flow rates
5. The eShunt's one-way valve is a PASSIVE CHECK VALVE — it responds to the instantaneous pressure differential but does NOT limit flow, adjust threshold, or adapt to patient-specific dynamics

The eShunt's venous position is an ADVANTAGE (lower baseline gradient than VP shunts), but its passive valve does NOT exploit this advantage for adaptive regulation.
what_the_residual_is_NOT: NOT claiming 'VP shunts cannot do this' (unsupported — removed in Round 35)
NOT claiming the eShunt is bad (it shows 97% improvement in NPH at 90 days)
NOT claiming a specific mechanism is novel (mechanism = UNPROPOSED)
NOT claiming over-drainage is unsolved by ALL technology (it is partially solved)
NOT claiming the eShunt's passive valve is the same as a VP shunt valve (the venous position is different)
evidence_gaps_that_remain: The eShunt's long-term (>90 day) over-drainage rate is UNKNOWN (STRIDE data pending)
The exact incidence of sigmoid sinus venous pressure drops during upright posture is not well-characterized
The 2026 anti-siphon meta-analysis showed subdural improvement but not overall over-drainage — the clinical importance of the residual needs source-binding
Whether the eShunt's venous position provides BETTER over-drainage protection than VP shunts (due to smaller hydrostatic gradient) is hypothesized but NOT yet demonstrated
residual_failure.gate_verdict: YELLOW — the residual failure is PLAUSIBLE and SPECIFIC, but NOT YET SOURCE-BOUND. The falsifiable causal statement is defined. The next step is to source-bind the evidence gaps before any mechanism generation.
